name: Naming the Crime: Genocide in the Twentieth Century
description: The mass murders of whole peoples, from the Armenians to the Holocaust, Cambodia, Bosnia and Rwanda, and the slow building of laws and courts to name and punish them.

checkpoints.name: Rules for war
checkpoints.note: The first Geneva Conventions of 1864 protect wounded soldiers on the battlefield. States begin to agree rules for how armies fight each other, but no law yet protects a people from its own rulers, as the old Ottoman Empire grows weaker and its minorities more exposed.

checkpoints.name: Deportation and famine
checkpoints.note: During World War I the Ottoman government deports and kills Armenians in huge numbers, a crime many states call the Armenian genocide and Turkey disputes. In the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin, the Holodomor famine of 1932 and 1933 kills millions in Ukraine, which many countries recognise as a genocide.

checkpoints.name: A world at war
checkpoints.note: In the Second Sino-Japanese War the army of the Empire of Japan captures Nanjing, and the Nanjing Massacre follows. Nazi Germany murders some six million Jews in the Holocaust, many at Auschwitz, and kills Roma, disabled people and others. In 1944 a new word, genocide, is coined to describe such crimes.

checkpoints.name: Law after the war
checkpoints.note: The trials at Nuremberg and Tokyo judge leaders for crimes against peace and humanity. In December 1948 the United Nations makes genocide a crime in international law and, a day later, adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Israel tries Adolf Eichmann in 1961, the year Amnesty International is founded.

checkpoints.name: The killing fields
checkpoints.note: From 1975 to 1979 the Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot cause the deaths of well over a million Cambodians. As Yugoslavia breaks apart, the Yugoslav Wars bring the expulsion and killing of civilians in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1994 about a hundred days of slaughter in the Rwandan genocide kill hundreds of thousands of Tutsi.

checkpoints.name: Courts and judgements
checkpoints.note: In 1995 Bosnian Serb forces kill about eight thousand Bosniak men and boys in eastern Bosnia, a massacre later judged a genocide. United Nations courts for Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia convict leaders, Pol Pot dies in 1998 without trial, and in 2018 a court in Cambodia convicts two Khmer Rouge leaders of genocide.
